site.tagline: Six seconds of film history. Twenty seconds of why it matters.

films.title: Nosferatu
films.scene_description: Count Orlok looms into Ellen's room at the window, rising into the clawed-hand silhouette that became the film's signature image.
films.commentary: This single pose — Schreck's silhouette, fingers splayed into claws against the window light — is the most reproduced image from the entire film, used on posters and in textbooks ever since. Murnau builds to it with almost a minute of unbroken tension, then holds the shape just long enough to burn it into memory.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1922, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari
films.scene_description: Caligari hypnotically calls the somnambulist Cesare out of his trance in one sustained close-up, just before unveiling him to the fairground crowd.
films.commentary: Conrad Veidt holds this single unbroken close-up for the better part of a minute, letting the kohl-rimmed eyes and painted-on shadows do all the acting — no cuts, no reaction shots, just Caligari's voice calling him out of the dark. It's one of the earliest horror films to trust stillness over movement to unsettle an audience.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1920, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The General
films.scene_description: A full-size steam locomotive plunges through a burning bridge in a single unfaked take.
films.commentary: That's not a miniature — Keaton actually dropped a full locomotive through a burning bridge, once, on camera, with no retakes possible. It was the single most expensive shot of the entire silent era. No stunt double, no trick photography, just a director who insisted the danger had to be real.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1926, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: His Girl Friday
films.scene_description: Hildy and Walter trade rapid, overlapping dialogue in his editor's office as he works to talk her out of quitting.
films.commentary: Hawks clocked this dialogue at nearly 240 words a minute, with actors deliberately talking over each other's lines. Most screenplays don't survive that; his did, because the overlaps were scripted, not improvised. It's still the reference point for fast-talking comedy, from Gilmore Girls to Aaron Sorkin's entire career.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use — renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case.

films.title: Night of the Living Dead
films.scene_description: Johnny mock-scares his sister with "They're coming to get you, Barbara" moments before the film's first real attack.
films.commentary: Romero shot this on a shoestring in rural Pennsylvania, and the grainy 16mm newsreel look wasn't a style choice — it's just what a $114,000 budget gets you. That accidental realism is what made it terrifying. It also invented the modern zombie outright; the word "zombie" never appears in the script.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain immediately upon release because the distributor's title-card change dropped the copyright notice, which US law at the time required.

films.title: Metropolis
films.scene_description: The robot double of Maria is brought to life in rings of light.
films.commentary: This transformation was built with practical light rings and in-camera exposure tricks decades before CGI existed — nobody has fully reverse-engineered Lang's exact method. The robot itself became the template for basically every sci-fi android after it, C-3PO included. A hundred years old and it still looks expensive.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired for the original 1927 release (published well past the 95-year term).
films.pd_caveat: The only prints readily available are the 2010 "complete" restoration, which adds newly rediscovered footage of its own. This clip is limited to the robot-transformation shot specifically, which was already present in every prior public-domain cut — a plain rescan of pre-existing PD frames is unlikely to carry its own copyright, but confirm before commercial use, and avoid pulling clips from this print's newly-restored scenes.
